subject: Pharmacology
summary: Cell‑cycle‑specific (CCS) drugs target cancer cells only when they are actively dividing in a particular phase of the cell cycle. By contrast, non‑cell‑cycle‑specific agents affect cells in any phase, including resting (G0) cells.

sections.p: CCS drugs are chemotherapeutic agents that exert cytotoxicity only during a defined phase of the cell‑cycle (e.g., S‑phase antimetabolites, M‑phase vinca alkaloids). Diagnosis is conceptual – recognizing which agents belong to this class guides regimen selection.
b: Identify the drug’s target phase (S, G2, M).
Distinguish CCS from NCCS drugs.

sections.p: Severity is not staged for the drug class itself; instead, clinicians assess tumour burden, performance status, and organ function to decide if a CCS regimen is appropriate.
b: Use ECOG or Karnofsky scores for patient fitness.
Consider tumour proliferation index (Ki‑67) to predict CCS efficacy.

sections.p: The “cause” is the choice of chemotherapy based on tumour biology. Highly proliferative tumours (e.g., acute leukaemia, lymphoma, germ‑cell tumours) are most likely to respond to CCS agents.
b: Rapidly dividing cancers → CCS drugs most effective.
Low‑proliferation tumours → NCCS agents preferred.

sections.p: Clinically, the effect of CCS drugs appears as tumour shrinkage after several cell‑cycle passages, often accompanied by phase‑specific toxicities such as myelosuppression (S‑phase) or neurotoxicity (M‑phase).
b: Delayed response – usually 2‑3 weeks after start.
Toxicities reflect the targeted phase.

sections.p: Laboratory and imaging tests help confirm that the tumour is proliferating and monitor drug effect.

t.b: What is the tumour proliferation rate? High Ki‑67 (>20%) supports use of CCS drugs.
Is bone‑marrow suppression occurring? Falling neutrophils indicate S‑phase drug toxicity.
Are organ functions adequate for drug metabolism and excretion? Abnormalities may require dose adjustment or alternative agents.

sections.p: Because CCS drugs act only on dividing cells, they spare resting tissues but can cause severe myelosuppression, mucositis, and neurotoxicity, which may become life‑threatening.
b: Febrile neutropenia → urgent antibiotics.
Severe peripheral neuropathy → stop vinca alkaloids.

sections.p: Select a CCS agent that matches the tumour’s growth phase, then provide supportive care to mitigate predictable toxicities.
b: Antimetabolites (e.g., 5‑FU, cytarabine) for S‑phase tumours – inhibit DNA synthesis.
Vinca alkaloids (e.g., vincristine) for M‑phase – disrupt microtubules.
Avoid overlapping neurotoxic drugs with vinca alkaloids.
Use growth‑factor support (G‑CSF) for profound neutropenia.
Hydration and allopurinol for tumour‑lysis risk with rapid‑kill CCS agents.

sections.p: Regular CBCs, renal/hepatic panels, and imaging assess response and toxicity. Prevent complications with prophylactic antibiotics, anti‑emetics, and dose‑adjustments based on organ function.
b: CBC weekly during the first two cycles.
Renal function before each dose of high‑dose antimetabolites.

sections.p: Non‑cell‑cycle‑specific (NCCS) drugs such as alkylating agents (cyclophosphamide) and anthracyclines (doxorubicin) which kill cells in any phase, including G0.
b: NCCS agents cause broader toxicity (e.g., alopecia, cardiotoxicity).
CCS agents are more phase‑selective.

sections.p: A low Ki‑67 may falsely suggest a tumour will not respond to CCS drugs, yet some tumours have heterogeneous proliferation that still benefits from CCS therapy.
b: Do not rely on a single biopsy; consider repeat sampling if clinical response is poor.

faq.q: Why do CCS drugs spare normal tissues?
faq.a: Most normal adult cells are in G0; CCS agents only act on cells actively cycling, so resting tissues are relatively protected.

faq.q: Can a tumour become resistant to CCS drugs?
faq.a: Yes, by slowing its proliferation rate or up‑regulating drug‑efflux pumps, making the cells less likely to be in the target phase.

faq.q: When should I choose an NCCS drug over a CCS drug?
faq.a: When the tumour shows low proliferation, has a high proportion of G0 cells, or when the patient cannot tolerate phase‑specific toxicities.

exam: Explain the pharmacologic rationale for using antimetabolites in S‑phase‑dependent tumours.
List two major toxicities of M‑phase vinca alkaloids and how you would monitor for them.
Differentiate cell‑cycle‑specific from non‑cell‑cycle‑specific chemotherapy in terms of mechanism and clinical implications.
